Spend
spĕnd
v. (to lay out or consume; to pass, as time; rendering Hebrew kalah, shaqal, Greek dapanao)
From Latin expendo, to weigh out. What is spent is weighed out and gone, and Scripture asks of every expenditure — of money, of days, of a life — what was bought with it.

Biblical Definition

To spend is to lay out what one has, and Scripture presses the question of what is bought. Isaiah puts it to a people spending on the wrong things: “Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness” (Isaiah 55:2). The rebuke is not against spending but against the purchase: money laid out for what is not bread, labour for what does not satisfy. Days are spent as surely as coin, and Moses measures them without flattery: “For all our days are passed away in thy wrath: we spend our years as a tale that is told” (Psalm 90:9). A whole life goes the way a story goes — told, and over. Job describes the prosperous who spend well by every visible measure and arrive nowhere: “They spend their days in wealth, and in a moment go down to the grave” (Job 21:13). And the prodigal's ruin is dated precisely from the moment his spending ended: “And when he had spent all, there arose a mighty famine in that land; and he began to be in want” (Luke 15:14). The famine was already coming; the spending merely removed his cushion against it.

Webster 1828 Definition

To lay out; to dispose of; to part with; to consume; to pass, as time. Scripture asks what a man's money and days purchase, warns of spending for what is not bread, and dates the prodigal's want from the moment he had spent all.

expand to see more

SPEND, v.t. [L. expendo, to weigh out.] To lay out; to dispose of; to part with; as, to spend money for clothing.

2. To consume; to waste; to squander; as, to spend an estate in gaming.

3. To bestow for any purpose; to employ; as, to spend one's labor or pains.

4. To pass, as time; to suffer to pass away; as, to spend a day or a year.

5. To exhaust of force or strength; as, a spent ball; the storm is spent.

SPEND, v.i. To make expense; to lay out or consume money or other property; also, to be consumed or wasted.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 55:2 — "Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness."

Psalm 90:9 — "For all our days are passed away in thy wrath: we spend our years as a tale that is told."

Job 21:13 — "They spend their days in wealth, and in a moment go down to the grave."

Luke 15:14 — "And when he had spent all, there arose a mighty famine in that land; and he began to be in want."

Modern Corruption

Spending is now audited only for value received in this life, so Isaiah's question — why lay out money for what is not bread — is answered by better shopping rather than by a different appetite.

expand to see more

Isaiah 55:2 asks a question that sounds financial and is not. The prophet is addressing men who are getting exactly what they paid for and remain unfed, and his remedy is not thrift but a different table: hearken diligently, eat that which is good, let your soul delight itself in fatness. Where the question is heard as counsel about budgeting, it is answered by spending more wisely on the same class of goods, and the soul goes on unsatisfied at a better price. The corruption is not extravagance; it is the assumption that satisfaction is purchasable at all, which the whole chapter exists to deny.

Psalm 90:9 and Job 21:13 press the same audit on time, which is the one currency no man can stop spending. Moses does not say our years are stolen or wasted; he says they are spent, laid out as a tale is told, and he draws from it the prayer to be taught to number our days. Job's prosperous men spend theirs in wealth and go down in a moment. The prodigal's case joins both threads: he spent all, and the famine that was coming anyway found him with nothing. Scripture's counsel is not to spend less but to know what is being bought, since the expenditure continues whether it is examined or not.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kalah (to finish, to consume) and shaqal (to weigh out money) supply the Old Testament senses; Greek dapanao (to spend, to consume) governs the prodigal's account.

expand to see more

Hebrew kalah (H3615) — to complete, to consume, to spend; used of years spent and strength consumed.

Hebrew shaqal (H8254) — to weigh out; the verb behind “spend money” in Isaiah 55:2, money being weighed silver.

Hebrew hegeh (H1899) — a moaning, a tale, a meditation; the “tale that is told” of Psalm 90:9.

Greek dapanao (G1159) — to spend, to consume, to squander; the prodigal's verb in Luke 15:14.

Greek ekdapanao (G1550) — to spend utterly, to exhaust; Paul's word for being spent for the souls of others.

Usage

"“Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread?” — the question is about appetite, not budgeting."

"“We spend our years as a tale that is told” — time is laid out whether or not it is counted."

"“When he had spent all… he began to be in want” — the famine was already coming."
